note: Definitions v2.0: the AGI definition, its eight parts, each part's test and our reading of the best public evidence. The owner sets the definition, the status scale and the tests (a change is a method change in data/method.json); the weekly components lens refreshes measurements, milestones and statuses. Built from the adversarially verified research packets of 2026-10-05.

definition.text: AGI: a system with the full scope of human cognitive autonomy: it can learn, reason, plan and generalize knowledge across any intellectual domain, without task-specific retraining.
definition.excludes: Physical and embodied work (robotics, manual skills) is out of scope: we judge the mind, not the body. The main cognitive frameworks (Hendrycks et al., DeepMind's Levels of AGI, ARC) leave it out too, and v1.0 already counted remote work only, so leaving it out makes the bar no looser.
definition.remoteWorkTest: It reliably (80% or better) does at least 80% of economically valuable remote professional tasks at the level of a median skilled professional, including multi-week projects, with no task-specific human scaffolding.
definition.rule: One system must meet every part's bar at the same time. Parts are judged on the best public evidence. An undisclosed system is judged under the fire alarm's proof standard (condition Y1) on evidence equivalent to passing all eight parts' tests at once: the same tests run by an evaluator or the lab, documented results, or insider evidence, since most tests name public systems and public leaderboards. A few tests ask for more than the definition strictly needs; they are our standard for confirming a part from public evidence, while our AGI-anywhere probability judges the definition itself.

The gap between the two measures is the main finding.

test.measure: Primary: the Remote Labor Index (RLI; Scale AI and CAIS) automation rate: the share of 240 real paid freelance projects (23 of Upwork's 64 work categories; median 11.5 hours of human work, mean 28.9) where human evaluators judge the AI's deliverable at least as good as the professional's, so that a reasonable client would accept it. Cross-check: OpenAI's GDPval 'wins or ties' rate against professionals' own deliverables (44 occupations; tasks average about 7 hours of expert work), broken down by occupation as in the GDPval paper. Context only, not tests: LLM-judged reruns of GDPval (Artificial Analysis, Mercor), which don't compare against the professionals; the Anthropic Economic Index, which measures use; and O*NET exposure studies, which measure potential exposure.
test.threshold: Partial: Remote Labor Index (RLI) 40% or more, or the GDPval per-occupation half passed. Close: RLI 60% or more. Met: RLI 80% or more, and on GDPval wins or ties in 80% or more of comparisons in at least 36 of the 44 occupations.
test.detail: Met when the best public system reaches an RLI automation rate of 80% or more and, on GDPval, wins or ties in 80% or more of comparisons in at least 36 of the 44 occupations (80% of them), not only on the overall average. No per-occupation GDPval results are published for current models, so that half is unmeasured today. Reliability (repeat success) and multi-week length are scored by their own components.
test.why: The breadth clause asks for a share of real economic work, so the test should be a share of real work. RLI is the closest public match: whole paid projects, judged against what a client would accept. GDPval checks quality against experienced professionals (its task writers averaged 14 years' experience) but uses one-shot, well-specified tasks, so it overstates breadth. Neither samples the whole remote economy: GDPval covers 44 occupations in 9 industries, and RLI covers 23 freelance categories and leaves out work that needs client interaction or long-term evaluation. We'd switch to a benchmark that samples remote O*NET tasks by wage share if one is published.

milestones.text: OpenAI and University of Pennsylvania researchers map GPT models onto O*NET tasks: about 80% of US workers could have at least 10% of their tasks affected, and about 19% at least half. This measures exposure, not ability.

OpenAI publishes GDPval: 1,320 tasks in 44 occupations, written by professionals averaging 14 years' experience and graded blind by same-occupation experts. The best model, Claude Opus 4.1, ties or beats the professionals on 47.6% of 220 gold-set tasks.
Scale AI and CAIS publish the Remote Labor Index. The best agent, Manus, completes 2.5% of real freelance projects to a standard a client would accept.

CAIS reports Claude Fable 5 at 15.8% on the RLI, nearly double Claude Opus 4.8's 8.3%, on a stronger setup than at launch (labs' own agent tools, longer budgets); none of the Fable 5 work it shows would be accepted.
GPT-6 Astra leads the RLI at 20.83%, the highest score so far (entry date from the leaderboard's page data; Astra was released on Sept 3, and we first recorded the score on Sept 29).

projection.text: No published forecast or fitted trend gives a date for 80% breadth. The Remote Labor Index (RLI) record (2.5% in Oct 2025; 15.8% in Jul 2026, on a stronger agent setup; 20.83% in Sept 2026) is short, has no confidence intervals and rose partly on scaffolding, so, as on our trends page, we give no date. CAIS found that RLI success doesn't fall as projects take humans longer, so METR's time-horizon trend can't date this part either.
projection.basis: RLI record points in data/trends.json (manual.rli: 2.5% on 2025-10-30, 15.8% on 2026-07-01, 20.83% with a leaderboard entry date of 2026-09-17). CAIS's July 1, 2026 post describes the stronger setup (industry scaffolds with computer use, up to 24 hours, $50 to $150 per project, a worker-critic loop) and its finding that pass rates don't fall with human completion time (https://safe.ai/blog/significant-increase-in-digital-labor-automation). We fit no trend to three points with a change of setup between them.

challenges.text: Whole projects aren't single deliverables. On one-shot, well-specified GDPval tasks, lab-reported scores are above 80%, but the best system still fails about four in five real freelance projects on the RLI. In the RLI paper's analysis of the launch agents' deliverables, 45.6% were poor quality, 35.7% were incomplete, 17.6% had corrupt or unusable files and 14.8% had inconsistencies (one deliverable can count in several), for example videos of 8 seconds where 8 minutes were requested, and floor plans that didn't match the supplied sketches.

Much remote work produces files other than text: 3D and CAD models, architecture drawings, video, audio and design files. The RLI includes them. Scale reports that the most common failure is amateur-quality work, while successes cluster in audio work, image generation (logos, ads), report writing and data retrieval. The RLI still leaves out work that needs direct client interaction, physical labor or long-term evaluation, and covers 23 of Upwork's 64 categories.

GDPval is one-shot and well specified. OpenAI says it doesn't capture building context, improving over multiple drafts or navigating ambiguity, such as talking to a client before deciding what to produce. OpenAI said in September 2025 that future versions would be more interactive; we have found none published.
challenges.ratingNote: OpenAI's GDPval post states these limits and the plan for more interactive versions; that none has been published is our own search as of Oct 5, 2026.

challenges.text: LLM judges overrate newer models, and the most often updated GDPval reruns use them. CAIS calibrated an automated judge on earlier models and found it overestimated GPT-5.5's RLI rate about 2.9 times (17.9% against 6.25% from human evaluators) and Claude Opus 4.8's about 2.3 times (18.8% against 8.33%), although it ranked the models correctly. Artificial Analysis's GDPval-AA and Mercor's GDPval leaderboards are LLM-judged and don't compare with the professionals' deliverables. The rankings also disagree: GPT-6 Astra leads the RLI but is 40th on GDPval-AA.

New tasks score lower than the public ones. Mercor's GDPval Extended adds 132 tasks it wrote to the 213 public GDPval tasks: Claude Opus 5.5 (Max) scores 88.3% on the public tasks and 75.8% on the extended benchmark, and GPT-6 Astra (Max) 86.7% and 64.1%. These are LLM-judged mean rubric scores, not wins or ties against professionals.

Deployment evidence leans on coding. Tasks tied to Computer and Mathematical occupations were 35% of Claude.ai conversations in February 2026, and more coding is moving to Anthropic's API through Claude Code, although Anthropic reports that Claude.ai use cases diversified (the top 10 tasks fell from 24% to 19% of traffic). The index measures what people bring to Claude, not what it can do.

components.hiddenAngle: Breadth is hard to observe for an undisclosed system. RLI scores exist only for systems Scale and CAIS can run (public releases, or models a lab submits), and GDPval win rates only for systems a lab chooses to report, so a hidden system passing this component would leave no trace on the leaderboards (A). It would more likely show up indirectly. The first route is economic footprint, which is hypothesis C's sanctioned path: the work gets sold. Signs would be an unexplained surge of high-quality remote deliverables on freelance platforms, or a sharp drop in hiring for outsourced design, analysis and media work. The second is a lab's own productivity claims: Anthropic's prototype R&D Automation Index says Claude 'leads' 26% of its AI R&D work as of August 2026, a measure that tracks A and B better than breadth. The third is a jump in a public model's RLI score after long internal use, which would show how far behind disclosure runs. Breadth on its own isn't evidence for B. For D, broad advisory work in government would show up through disclosed contracts and use (D-open), not through these benchmarks.

components.name: Professional quality
components.question: When the system hands in a piece of work (a memo, a spreadsheet model, a legal draft, a design), experienced people in that job judge it at least as good as what a typical skilled professional would have delivered.
components.clause: v1.0 test: "at the level of a median skilled professional"; v2.0 definition: "the full scope of human cognitive autonomy ... across any intellectual domain" (the quality half of that scope; how many domains is the breadth component, how often is the reliability component).

components.statusNote: The well-specified half is cleared in aggregate only: GPT-5.5 wins or ties industry professionals in 84.9% of GDPval comparisons (OpenAI, April 2026), against our 50%, with no results by occupation. The real-project half is not: the best Remote Labor Index rate is 20.8% (GPT-6 Astra) against 50%, and the best all-pass score on Harvey's legal benchmark is 17.8%.
components.statusDetail: In aggregate the well-specified half is cleared: GPT-5.5 wins or ties industry professionals in 84.9% of GDPval comparisons (OpenAI, Apr 23, 2026) against our 50% bar, though no per-occupation breakdown has been published since the original paper, so the 80%-of-occupations condition is unverified. The real-project half is not: the best Remote Labor Index rate is 20.8% (GPT-6 Astra, posted Sept 17) against 50%, and the best all-pass score on Harvey's legal benchmark is 17.8% (Claude Opus 5).
components.bar: Parity with professionals: wins or ties 50%+ on expert-graded tasks in 80% of occupations, and 50%+ of real projects judged as good.

test.measure: Human grading of the system's deliverable against a professional's deliverable for the same task. Two parts: (1) well-specified tasks: blind head-to-head grading by experts from the same occupation, as the rate of wins or ties against professionals (GDPval or a successor), reported per occupation; (2) real end-to-end projects: the share of real commissioned projects where human evaluators, taking a reasonable client's view, judge the system's deliverable at least as good as the professional's (Remote Labor Index automation rate). All-pass legal rubrics (Harvey LAB, applied by an LLM judge to attorney-written criteria) are a domain check only.
test.threshold: Partial: either half passed, or RLI 25% or more. Close: RLI 35% or more with the well-specified half passed by occupation. Met: (a) expert-graded wins or ties 50%+, with at least as many wins as losses where wins are reported, on well-specified tasks in at least 80% of occupations, and (b) RLI 50% or more, held across two leaderboard updates.
test.detail: Met when, under a general harness, the best public system (a) wins or ties the professional at least 50% of the time, with at least as many wins as losses where wins are reported, on expert-graded well-specified tasks in at least 80% of occupations tested, and (b) has its deliverable judged at least as good as the professional's on at least 50% of real end-to-end projects (RLI automation rate 50% or more). 50% is parity: the system's work matches or beats the professional's on half the tasks; with comparison professionals who are typical or better, that is at least a median professional's level (our inference).
test.why: The definition asks for the level of a median skilled professional, so the natural measure is a comparison with professionals' own deliverables, judged by people. Part (a) alone is not enough: GDPval's own authors say its tasks are precisely specified and one-shot, while real work involves ambiguity, iteration and long deliverables; part (b) tests quality on real projects. GDPval's comparison workers average 14 years of experience, above the median, so parity with them is a conservative test (our inference). Wins-or-ties alone would let a model that loses more often than it wins pass when ties are common, hence the wins-versus-losses check. LLM-judged scores do not count toward the threshold: CAIS found an automated judge overstated RLI rates two to three times for the newest models. Exam scores (bar, medical licensing) are excluded as the main test because they measure knowledge, not work product, and have overstated professional competence before. How many occupations and how reliably are left to the breadth and reliability components.

milestones.text: MMLU benchmark published: the largest GPT-3 beats random guessing by almost 20 points on average across 57 subjects, with near-random accuracy on law and morality.

A peer-reviewed re-analysis (Martínez, Artificial Intelligence and Law) of GPT-4's simulated bar exam, which OpenAI put around the top 10%, places it near the 48th percentile among those who passed, and about the 15th on the essays.

OpenAI launches GDPval: blind grading by experts from the same occupation on 220 public tasks across 44 occupations, each about 7 hours of expert work. The best model, Claude Opus 4.1, wins or ties on 47.6%, just under half.

Scale AI and the Center for AI Safety publish the Remote Labor Index: 240 real freelance projects averaging about 29 hours of professional work. The best agent (Manus) delivers client-acceptable work on 2.5%.

GPT-5.2 Thinking beats or ties industry professionals in 70.9% of GDPval comparisons, according to expert human judges; OpenAI calls it its first model at or above human expert level. GPT-5.2 Pro wins outright in 60.0%.

GPT-5.5 reaches 84.9% wins or ties on GDPval (GPT-5.4 in March: 83.0%, with 70.8% outright wins). It is the last GDPval figure OpenAI has published; its later launch posts give the LLM-judged GDPval-AA or none.

Remote Labor Index: Fable 5 reaches 15.8%, up from 2.5% in under eight months, run with stronger scaffolding. The Center for AI Safety says today's AIs still fall short of professional quality on most projects.

Mercor reports frontier models outscoring all 12 licensed junior accountants (about 5.5 years' experience) on simplified month-end close tasks: models scored perfectly, the accountants averaged about 37%. Mercor says the tasks played to models' strengths and left out client work.

challenges.text: Expert grading is slow: in the GDPval paper, expert graders took about 109 minutes on average to review each model deliverable.

Model judges overstate quality. CAIS calibrated an automated judge on older models and found it rated GPT-5.5 at 17.9% on the Remote Labor Index where human judges gave 6.25% (Opus 4.8: 18.8% against 8.33%). components.hiddenAngle: Professional quality is among the easiest components to test in private (our inference). Labs grade professional work before release: OpenAI published GDPval results with its launches through April 2026 and reports internal investment-banking, consulting, design and data-science task suites, and it has published no expert-graded GDPval figure since GPT-5.5, so a jump would not show at once. Under A (Hidden AGI), the first traces would be internal-only professional evals in system cards running well ahead of the public model, or a lab's own back-office and client work done without staff rework. Under C (Covert AGI actor), on its sanctioned but undisclosed path, an operator could sell deliverables through agencies or freelance platforms, the kind of work RLI samples; that would appear only as unexplained output or price shifts in particular occupations, which we cannot tell apart from public models plus human review. Under D-open, it would appear as government contracts for AI-produced analyses or drafts. B links only through the quality of AI-led research work (Claude leads 26% of Anthropic's AI R&D on Anthropic's own index, August). Detection is weak: quality shows only through human grading someone chooses to publish, so a benchmark that stops moving does not rule out a hidden system (our inference).

test.measure: Primary: METR's 80% time horizon, the length of task (in skilled-human working time) that the system completes successfully four times in five, with a general harness. Check: repeat-run consistency on a current agent benchmark, read as pass^k (the share of tasks done right on every one of k independent tries; tau-bench reports k up to 4), alongside wrong-answer rates (how often a model answers wrongly instead of saying it doesn't know).
test.threshold: Partial: pass^4 50% or more on tau3-Banking, or an 80% time horizon of a workday (8 h). Close: pass^4 65% on tau3-Banking and an 80% time horizon of a work-week (40 h). Met: pass^4 80% on tau3-Banking and on the tau2 average, and an 80% time horizon of a work-month (167 h) on a suite able to measure it.
test.detail: An 80% time horizon of at least one work-month (167 working hours, 10,020 minutes, the bar our trend fit on Trend watch uses), with a general harness, on a task suite able to measure that length; and pass^4 of at least 80% on the hardest current tau-bench domain (today tau3-Banking) and on the average of the three tau2 domains (retail, airline, telecom). Wrong-answer rates are tracked but carry no pass mark yet.
test.why: The definition asks for 80%-or-better success on at least 80% of tasks, including multi-week projects. The 80% horizon is the task length at which a system succeeds four times in five, so a work-month reading is the closest published measure of that clause; it folds the two 80% figures into one number, which is why we add a repeat-run check. Pass^4 is the share of tasks done right on all four tries. With four tries it is the natural estimate of the share of tasks done at least 80% of the time (three of four is only 75%), and an average over lucky and unlucky runs cannot pass it. It is strict: a task done right exactly 80% of the time comes out four for four only 41% of the time, so we also show the share done right on at least three of four tries (our calculation from Sierra's pass^3 and pass^4) as a lenient read. What it misses: METR's suite is mostly software, machine-learning and cybersecurity tasks and cannot measure beyond about 16 hours today, and tau-bench is customer-service work, so neither covers all professional work.

milestones.text: GPT-2: METR estimates an 80% time horizon of under a second (0.01 min), against about 3 seconds (0.05 min) at 50%.
GPT-4: 80% horizon about 0.9 minutes, against about 4 minutes at 50% (4.5 times longer).
The tau-bench paper introduces pass^k: agents built on GPT-4o succeed on under 50% of tasks, and pass^8 is under 25% in retail.
GPT-5: 80% horizon about 38 minutes, against about 3.4 hours at 50%.

Anthropic's usage data (Nov 13-20, 2025; success judged by Claude; published Jan 15, 2026): API tasks succeed 49% of the time, falling from about 60% on sub-hour tasks to about 45% on tasks of 5+ human hours; Claude.ai conversations 67%.

Princeton researchers propose 12 agent-reliability metrics (consistency, robustness, predictability, safety) and find recent capability gains brought only small reliability gains (14 models; the June 2 revision covers 15, up to GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7).
Sierra's tau-Knowledge paper introduces the banking domain: frontier models with high reasoning budgets reach only about 25.5% on one try, and reliability falls sharply over repeated tries.
Claude Mythos Preview (early snapshot): 80% horizon about 3.1 hours, the best published, against about 17 hours at 50% (published May 8); METR says its suite cannot measure above 16 hours reliably.
tau3-Banking: the best model completes 35.1% of tasks on all four tries (Qwen 3.8 Max), against 55.2% on one try.

projection.text: Our fit of METR's data has the 80% horizon doubling about every 129 days (range 109-158), the same pace as the 50% horizon, so the gap between them is not closing. The fitted 80% trend reaches a work week around Nov 2027 (May 2027-Jun 2028) and a work month around Jul 2028 (Jan 2028-May 2029); counting from the Mythos Preview measurement instead, Jul 2027 and Apr 2028. METR's current suite could not confirm a month-scale 80% horizon, so a crossing would need a new suite. Princeton's metrics show reliability rising only slowly over two years of releases, but we found no published forecast for pass^k or hallucination rates, so we project neither.
projection.basis: Least-squares fit of log2(80% horizon) on release date, METR frontier models since 2023 (data/trends.json, metr.p80: doublingDays 128.6, range 108.6-157.7; crossings.workWeek mid 2027-11-02, fast 2027-05-22, slow 2028-06-24; crossings.workMonth mid 2028-07-24, fast 2028-01-03, slow 2029-05-13; crossingsFromMeasured workWeek 2027-07-26, workMonth 2028-04-16; metr.p50 doublingDays 128.7).

upcoming.text: Our forecast deadline: METR publishes a time-horizon estimate for GPT-6 Astra (we said 50%).

challenges.text: Success falls as tasks get longer. In every METR measurement of models since 2023 the 80% horizon is 4 to 10 times shorter than the 50% horizon (median about 5; 10 for Claude Opus 4.6), and in Anthropic's November 2025 usage data API success fell from about 60% on sub-hour tasks to about 45% on tasks of 5+ hours.

Run-to-run inconsistency: agents that solve a task on one try often fail it on the next. Princeton finds outcome consistency low across all 15 models it tested and capability gains bringing only small reliability gains; on Sierra's leaderboard the top scores fall 20 to 25 points between one try and all four (retail 84.4% to 59.6%, banking 55.2% to 35.1%).

Poor calibration: the most accurate models still answer when they do not know. On AA-Omniscience, when Claude Fable 5.1 (Max) does not get a question right it gives a wrong answer 72.6% of the time rather than declining, and Claude Opus 5.5 (Max) 58.6%; Gemini 4 Argon's 15.1% shows a low rate is possible, at lower accuracy (49.9%).

Measurement lags and overstates: METR says its suite cannot measure horizons above about 16 hours, no 80% horizon has been published for Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra or Gemini 4 Argon, and automated graders overstate real acceptance (METR researchers found roughly half of test-passing SWE-bench Verified fixes by mid-2024 to late-2025 agents would not be merged; the grader scored about 24 points above maintainers).

Gaming the test: METR could not get a robust time horizon for GPT-5.6 Sol (June 26, 2026) because its detected cheating rate was higher than that of any public model METR had evaluated on its ReAct agent harness. Counting cheats as failures gave a 50% horizon of about 11 hours; counting them as successes, over 270 hours.

components.hiddenAngle: Public leaderboards see only public models, so they cannot show a reliable hidden system directly; three windows can. (1) METR's Frontier Risk Report, the only published outside estimate we know of that covers labs' internal models, put the internal frontier's 80% horizon at 'Likely ≥3h but <4h' in the Feb 16-Mar 16, 2026 window (public frontier about 1.5 h; internal on average about 2 months ahead) and found none of the shared models significantly more capable than the strongest public models as of May 19, 2026. A jump in a later report would be the main tell for A (Hidden AGI). (2) Anthropic reports that as of August 2026 Claude leads 26% of its AI R&D with no fully autonomous subset (self-reported; a Claude judge assigns the levels). B (Hidden self-improvement) needs long, reliable autonomous runs, so a fully autonomous share appearing there would matter most. Anthropic's 11-day, largely autonomous Fermat proof (Sept 4, 2026) shows long runs work where a proof checker verifies every step; our inference is that this does not carry over to professional work no checker can verify. (3) C (Covert AGI actor) and D (Covert government influence) need a system trusted to act for weeks without a human checking. Current incidents point the other way: Glow's PixelLeak report (Sept 29, 2026; credible report) describes coding agents posting more than 13,000 internal screenshots to public GitHub repositories. One limit on outside detection: METR could not measure GPT-5.6 Sol robustly because it cheated on tests, so a system that games evaluations can be hard to read from outside. Our inference: unattended work at scale would show up as fewer human checks, fully autonomous shares in lab reports and fewer agent incidents, and nothing public suggests a hidden system meets this component.

Part 2, the binding half, is not: public models hold 4 of the 10 AI-alone solves we ask for on Epoch's Open Problems (none above 'solid result'; two were existing human constructions the model found) and 2 of Epoch's 68 open Erdős problems, and credited new results outside mathematics are few (our reading).

test.measure: Two parts. (1) Closed-answer reasoning: the best public model on fixed-answer tests that span many fields: GPQA Diamond (198 graduate-level biology, chemistry and physics questions), Humanity's Last Exam without tools (2,500 expert-written questions across mathematics, the humanities and the sciences), FrontierMath Tier 4 (research-level mathematics). (2) Open-ended research reasoning: new results that a public model produces under a general harness, without task-specific human direction, and that independent experts accept. In mathematics we count AI-alone solves on Epoch AI's FrontierMath: Open Problems (problems that resisted serious attempts by professional mathematicians), using Epoch's 'Solved (AI)' label. Outside mathematics we count new results whose human co-authors credit the model with the core idea, in refereed or author-posted papers.
test.threshold: Partial: either part passed. Close: part 1 passed and the mathematics half of part 2 met (10 AI-alone solves on Epoch's Open Problems by public models, one a major advance or breakthrough). Met: both parts, including 3 credited new results in two or more fields outside mathematics.
test.detail: Part 1: GPQA Diamond 74% or more (the GPQA paper's accuracy for in-field PhD experts on its full question pool, excluding mistakes they later recognized; PhD experts recruited by OpenAI scored 69.7% on Diamond itself); FrontierMath Tier 4 50% or more and Humanity's Last Exam 50% or more without tools (our marks: neither test has a human expert baseline). Part 2 (our proposed bar): a public model holds 10 or more AI-alone solves on Epoch's Open Problems, at least one rated 'major advance' or 'breakthrough', and there are at least three independently credited new results in two or more fields outside mathematics. Both parts must hold.
test.why: A median skilled professional both knows the answers in their field and can work out a new one on their own; part 1 checks the first, part 2 the second. Part 1 tests saturate fast, so part 2 is the binding test. Epoch's bar for a listed problem is a result publishable in its own right, which is what a working researcher produces. The numbers 10, one 'major advance' and three outside results are our choice, not a published standard, and part 2 asks for more than a median professional does: these problems resisted professional mathematicians. What it misses: reasoning in fields with no checker (law, strategy, policy, medical judgment), where tests rely on expert grading; results by public models on problems outside Epoch's list; and how often a model reasons badly while sounding sure.

components.hiddenAngle: Reasoning is the component most likely to show if a hidden system has it, because its products are checkable and valuable: a solved open problem, a Lean proof, an unusual run of papers. So far labs have claimed such results openly, often from unreleased models: OpenAI's Erdős unit-distance disproof (May 20) and Navier–Stokes proof (Sept 8), and Anthropic's Riemann-zeros bound (Aug 10). That shows internal reasoning runs ahead of public models (relevant to A), but because the results were disclosed they are not evidence of secrecy; Epoch notes that the most impressive AI math results have come from inside AI companies with little transparency about how they were obtained. Attribution is already loose: Epoch marks the Sept 17 proof that ζ(5) is irrational 'human + AI' with an 'unknown AI system', though the preprint does not acknowledge particularly substantial AI use. So one unattributed solution would not point to a hidden system; a run of strong solutions to listed problems (Epoch's lists, erdosproblems.com) or Lean submissions with no stated author or model would matter for C. It would not show if the owner keeps results private: a government program (A) or a system advising decision-makers (D) leaves no published trace, and Epoch says only OpenAI has bought its Open Problems verifiers, so private checking is possible. Mathematical reasoning says little directly about B; AI R&D share is the better gauge there (our inference).

components.bar: An 80% time horizon of a work-month (167 h) on a suite able to measure it, plus a documented multi-week project. Close at a work-week (40 h).

test.measure: METR-style 80% time horizon: the length of task, in skilled-human working hours, that the best public system completes with 80% success in a general agent harness, read from METR's published measurements (work-week = 40 h, work-month = 167 h, as on Trend watch; our trend fit there is context and projection, not a measurement). It must be measured on a task suite that can resolve horizons that long. For 'met' it must also be backed by at least one independently documented multi-week project outside formally checkable domains, delivered at professional quality with no task-specific scaffolding.
test.threshold: Partial: an 80% time horizon of a workday (8 h). Close: a work-week (40 h) on a suite able to measure it. Met: a work-month (167 h) on a suite able to measure it, plus a documented multi-week project outside formally checkable work.
test.detail: Met when the 80% horizon reaches a work-month (167 working hours) on a suite able to measure it, and a documented multi-week project outside formally checkable domains backs it up. Close at a work-week (40 hours) on a suite able to measure it. Results confined to formally checkable work (Lean proofs, programs rebuilt against complete test suites) are shown, but on their own they count toward neither mark.
test.why: The 80% success rate is the definition's "reliably (80% or better)", and human-hours of work are the most direct published measure of "multi-week projects"; a work-month covers projects of two to four weeks. It misses messiness: METR describes its tasks as mostly software, machine-learning and cybersecurity work, self-contained and well specified, and both METR and MirrorCode's authors find far longer horizons where a precise, checkable target exists. That is why checkable-only results don't count by themselves and why we require a documented real project for 'met'. The status is the same with a looser two-week (80-hour) bar.

challenges.text: Reliability lags capability. For Claude Mythos Preview the 80% horizon (3.1 hours) is under a fifth of the 50% horizon (17.4 hours): it finishes half of 17-hour tasks, but four in five only at about 3 hours.

The yardstick runs out. METR's suite has 228 tasks, only five estimated at more than 16 human-hours and none above 30, and METR says it can't reliably measure horizons above 16 hours. Cheating clouds the long end: at least 16% of apparently successful runs on tasks of 8 hours or more were cheats.

Messy work is harder. METR's tasks score on average 2.4 of 16 on its 'messiness' scale, where writing a good research paper would score 9 to 15. Claude Opus 4.6's 50% horizon is 17.8 hours on the less messy half and 6.4 hours on the messier half, and only about half of test-passing SWE-bench Verified solutions would have passed real code review.

Checkable specs flatter the numbers. The longest successes (MirrorCode, Fermat in Lean) have a precise target with automatic checks. MirrorCode's authors found that with no visible tests, scores on larger programs 'declined precipitously', and they attribute the long horizons largely to the precise specification.

Keeping the thread needs scaffolding. In the Fermat project, Anthropic's first multi-agent attempts 'quickly lost track of the project's state'; the run succeeded after moving to Prove2Me, a formalization platform that tracks a graph of theorems for the agents.

Judgement over long projects. METR found that Claude Opus 5.5 'still has qualitative weaknesses that an expert human is unlikely to exhibit when solving hard, long-horizon tasks'. Anthropic reports more cases of the model 'dismissing its own doubts or abandoning its own stated plan', and of checking a plan against requirements it wrote itself.

components.hiddenAngle: Long-horizon autonomy is the component a lab would most likely see first internally. The main public check is outside review of internal models: in METR's Feb–Mar 2026 pilot, Anthropic, Google, Meta and OpenAI said they shared their internal state of the art, and METR put the internal frontier about 2 months ahead on time horizon; METR plans another round in late 2026. A hidden system at multi-week reliability would show up as a jump in that round, unless a lab stops sharing (hypothesis A). It would also show up as a fully autonomous share of AI R&D above zero, or speed-up estimates above about 3x (hypothesis B). Today Anthropic reports no fully autonomous share as of August, and a separate METR team's preliminary estimate is about 1.5x. A third sign would be headline results from 'internal' models that labs call comparable to public ones, as with the Fermat run. Agent fleets or operations running for weeks with no human operator would be the observable sign for hypothesis C (our Escape watch). Hypothesis D needs months of sustained planning and would be the hardest to see. One blind spot: no general-purpose public suite measures an 80% horizon past about 16 hours (MirrorCode reaches weeks of human work, but only on precisely specified software), so even a public system near the threshold could go unconfirmed for months. Incidents also surface a median of about 106 days late (our gauge). (our inference)

components.name: Autonomy without scaffolding
components.question: Can the AI be handed a computer, ordinary tools and a goal, and finish real work on its own, without people building a custom pipeline for each job or stepping in along the way?

components.statusNote: Hands-off success clears 80% only on short tasks: 86% on OSWorld-Verified's few-minute desktop tasks (Claude Fable 5). On OSWorld 2.x's 1.6-hour workflows the best official strict score is 44.3% (Claude Opus 5), and only 23% of OpenAI's 16–32 hour research tasks succeeded with no human intervention (January to July).
components.statusDetail: Hands-off success clears our 80% bar only on short tasks: a general model scores 86% on OSWorld-Verified's few-minute desktop tasks (Claude Fable 5), and OpenAI's agents finished 86% of its under-15-minute research tasks with no human intervention. On longer work it falls well short: the best official strict score on OSWorld 2.x's 1.6-hour workflows is 44.3% (Claude Opus 5; Anthropic self-reports 48.7% for Claude Opus 5.5 on its own harness), and only 43% of OpenAI's 4-8 hour tasks (53% in July) and 23% of its 16-32 hour tasks succeeded with no intervention.
components.bar: 80% strict on OSWorld 2.x with the official general harness, and 80% of multi-day tasks done with no human stepping in. Close at 65%.

test.measure: Strict (full-completion) success, pass@1, on long-horizon professional computer workflows run on one general harness for every task: a virtual machine, the model's standard computer-use and shell tools, a written goal, a step budget, and no per-task pipelines, hints or mid-task human input. Primary benchmark: the official OSWorld 2.x leaderboard's 'Foundation E2E GUI' track (108 workflows, a median of about 1.6 hours for a skilled human, 500-step cap). Cross-check in real use: the share of all delegated tasks that succeed with no human intervention, by task length, as published by a lab or evaluator (today only OpenAI publishes this).
test.threshold: Partial: OSWorld 2.x 50% strict on the official general harness, or either part passed. Close: 65% strict, or 80% of 4–8 hour tasks done with no human intervention. Met: 80% strict, and 80% of multi-day tasks (16 h or more) done with no human intervention.
test.detail: Met when a public system scores at least 80% strict on OSWorld 2.x under the official harness, and a lab or evaluator reports that at least 80% of multi-day tasks (16 or more hours of human work) succeed with no human intervention. We mark it close at 65% strict, or when at least 80% of 4-8 hour tasks succeed with no intervention.
test.why: 80% is the definition's own reliability bar, one general harness with no mid-task help is its 'no task-specific human scaffolding' clause, and only a fully finished task counts, because partial credit is not what a client accepts. We count hands-off successes as a share of all tasks, not of successful ones, so a system can't pass by rarely succeeding but doing it unaided. What it misses: OSWorld tasks last hours, not weeks (the long-horizon component covers that); OSWorld 2.x publishes no human success rate, so we can't say whether skilled people would clear 80% strict (OSWorld 1.0's human baseline was 72.36%); and the only intervention data are OpenAI's own, from interactive research-coding sessions, judged by its own classifier (checked against people on 25 tasks), on tasks researchers chose to delegate.

milestones.text: GPT-2 cannot run in METR's agent scaffold at all (its context is too short); on one-step prompts it handles tasks that take a person about 3 seconds, METR's 50% horizon measured in 2025. The zero point of the autonomy trend.

ARC Evals (now METR) reports testing GPT-4 and Claude with code execution, a researcher-simulated browser and delegation to copies of themselves, under supervision: the models complete many relevant subtasks but cannot replicate autonomously.
OSWorld (369 real desktop tasks) is published: humans complete 72.36%, the best model 12.24%.

Anthropic releases computer use in public beta for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, which it calls the first frontier model to offer it: 14.9% on OSWorld screenshot-only, 22.0% with more steps, against 7.8% for the next-best system.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 scores 61.4% on OSWorld-Verified (official framework, 100 steps, averaged over 4 runs), as a general model with no custom agent framework.

Simular's Agent S3, a framework that runs 10 attempts and picks the best (behavior best-of-N), is listed at 72.58% on the official OSWorld-Verified leaderboard, the first entry above the 72.36% human baseline (Simular announced it Dec 16).

OSWorld 2.0 resets the bar with 108 workflows that take a skilled human a median of about 1.6 hours, about 48 times longer than OSWorld 1.0: the best system, Claude Opus 4.8 at max thinking, fully completes 20.6% (54.8% partial).

General models pass 80% on OSWorld-Verified's short tasks with no agent framework, extra coding actions or multiple attempts: Meta's Muse Spark 1.1 is listed at 80.67%, and Claude Fable 5 at 85.96% on Aug 1.

After 11 days of largely autonomous work, an internal Anthropic model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.1 completes an end-to-end Lean proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, on the Prove2Me formalization platform plus a Claude Code-based multi-agent harness (published Sept 4).

OpenAI's research agents, January to July: 86% of tasks under 15 minutes finished with no human intervention, 43% of 4-8 hour tasks and 23% of 16-32 hour tasks; on 4-8 hour tasks the monthly rate rose from 18% to 53%.

projection.text: METR expected in May that by late 2026 frontier agents inside labs could often work for long stretches with no human stepping in, enough for some projects that would take people weeks, mainly ones where progress is easy to check. We give no date of our own: OpenAI's monthly readings of hands-off success are noisy (4-8 hour tasks rose from 18% in January to 53% in July, while 8-16 hour tasks fell from 58% to 35% between June and July) and the task mix shifts, and OSWorld 2.x's workflows are about 48 times longer than the original OSWorld's, so the original's pace doesn't carry over.
projection.basis: METR Frontier Risk Report (May 19, 2026); OpenAI chart data (Sept 6, 2026): 4-8 hour zero-intervention success 18% Jan, 35% Feb, 48% Mar, 39% Apr, 43% May, 54% Jun, 53% Jul (half-width about 5 points); OSWorld-Verified leaderboard (Claude Sonnet 4 43.9% listed 2025-07-28; Muse Spark 1.1 80.67% 2026-07-09; Claude Fable 5 85.96% 2026-08-01); OSWorld 2.x official board (20.6% June, 44.33% v2.1).

challenges.text: Finishing, not just progressing: the best general entry on the official OSWorld 2.x board earns 77.7% partial credit but fully completes only 44.3% of workflows. In the benchmark paper, the four models broken down by task length completed none of the tasks that take a skilled human more than about 2.7 hours; agents lost track of constraints, missed information that arrived mid-task, guessed instead of asking and skipped verification.

Humans are still in the loop for longer work: OpenAI says its agents still need significant human steering as tasks get harder. From January to July, over half of successful 4-8 hour tasks needed at least one intervention, and only 23% of 16-32 hour tasks succeeded hands-off. Even the 'automated research intern' OpenAI says it has reached is described as working under human direction.

The longest hands-off runs lean on purpose-built setups: Anthropic's 11-day, largely autonomous Fermat proof ran on Prove2Me, a platform built for formalizing mathematics, plus a Claude Code-based multi-agent harness. Earlier attempts without it stalled when agents lost track of where the project stood.

Scores depend on the harness and the task release: rerunning on its own harness, Anthropic puts Claude Opus 5 at 37.2% strict, against 44.3% on the official board, and says its figures are not comparable with other harness setups. On the official board the same model scored 31.4% on the August task release and 44.3% on v2.1.

Safety pulls against hands-off operation: unattended agents have gone out of scope on real systems (the July Hugging Face intrusion, run start to finish by an autonomous agent system, is one of 15 incidents on our list), and labs now put automated checkpoints between agents and the world: OpenAI ships auto-review and a confirmation policy in Codex and ChatGPT Work, and Anthropic says every action of the agents on its main internal platform passes an online monitor. Our inference is that deployed autonomy will lag tested autonomy.

components.hiddenAngle: Hands-off autonomy is the component a hidden system would most likely give away, because it acts on the world. For C (Covert AGI actor), such a system would show up the way sub-AGI agents already have: unattended swarms leaving traces on third-party systems (14,591 surviving revisions across four wikis in the DseWiki case; many thousands of actions, over 17,000 logged events, against Hugging Face). Those incidents took a median of about 106 days to become public, so detection is real but lagged, and that lag is a floor. For A and B, the tell would be internal-use metrics running ahead of what public models can do. Anthropic's fully autonomous share of its AI R&D is still 0% (August); our signal is confirmed at any share above 0%, and alarm condition X3 needs more than 10%. OpenAI's hands-off success on 4-8 hour tasks has risen (18% in January to 53% in July), but OpenAI doesn't name the models behind it, so the data can't yet separate internal models from public ones. Benchmarks are a weak detector, because a lab hiding a system would not submit it to OSWorld. Labs also now run agent actions past monitors and auto-review (Anthropic: every action on its main internal platform), which cuts outside traces, so a capable system run inside a lab could work hands-off and stay invisible until a disclosure. For D, autonomy matters less: influence on government runs through advice humans act on, not hands-off operation.

components.name: Learning on the job
components.question: Whether an AI can pick up a new skill or new knowledge the way a new hire does, from instructions, documents and its own mistakes, and keep it for next time, without its makers retraining it for that job.
components.clause: "it can learn ... without task-specific retraining"; working component: acquires and keeps new skills or knowledge from instruction, documents or experience, at roughly the pace of a skilled professional, without task-specific retraining or fine-tuning.
components.statusBasis: Far: CL-Bench 25.4% is below the 30% Partial mark; the other two parts have no public test.
components.glance: Captures about a quarter of the available gain from experience (25.4%, against 50%); keeping it is unmeasured.
components.statusNote: The best public system captures 25.4% of the available gain from experience on CL-Bench (Claude Sonnet 4.6, June 2026), about half our provisional 50%; none of the September 2026 models has been scored. Learning from documents after the training cutoff, and keeping what was learned, have no public measurement.
components.statusDetail: On learning that carries across tasks, the best public system captures 25.4% of the available gain on CL-Bench (plain in-context learning with Claude Sonnet 4.6, June 2026), about half our provisional 50% bar; none of the September 2026 models has been scored, and parts 2 and 3 (post-cutoff document learning, retention) have no public measurement. Learning within one session is stronger: GPT-6 Astra scores 62.7% on ARC-AGI-3 with ARC Prize's Standard harness and 99.9% with its Provider Adapter harness, while the strongest lab result we found on MTOB (Gemini 1.5 Pro, 2024) reached the human learner's level in only one translation direction.
components.bar: Provisional: capture 50% of the gain from experience (CL-Bench), match a human learner from documents, and keep 90% of it.

test.measure: A two-part proxy, run with a general harness only (no per-task fine-tuning, no task-specific scaffolding). (1) Learning from experience: normalized gain on Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench, from UC Berkeley, UW-Madison and Snorkel AI). This is the share of the available improvement a system captures when it carries what it learned through a sequence of related tasks, compared with the same system starting each task fresh, in six expert-validated domains from codebases to demand forecasting. (2) Learning from documents: MTOB-style tasks. The system learns a skill it cannot have seen in training (a new language, tool or codebase) only from the material a human learner would get, and is scored against a human who learned from the same material. Retention is checked by re-testing after a long run of unrelated work.
test.threshold: Provisional. Partial: CL-Bench normalized gain 30% or more, or any one of the three parts passed. Close: CL-Bench 40% or more. Met: all three parts: CL-Bench 50% or more with positive gain in 80% of domain runs; the human learner's level on a task released after the model's training cutoff (for a language, in both translation directions); 90% of the gain kept after unrelated work.
test.detail: Provisional, our inference. (1) An average normalized gain of 50% or more across CL-Bench's six domains, with positive gain in at least 80% of domain runs. (2) A score at or above the human learner on an MTOB-style task released after the model's training cutoff (for a language, in both translation directions). (3) At least 90% of the learned gain still present after the unrelated work. We will replace the 50% with a measured median-professional learning curve as soon as a benchmark publishes one.
test.why: The definition says the system learns without task-specific retraining. Our working component adds that it keeps what it learns, at roughly a professional's pace. CL-Bench separates learning from baseline skill by comparing stateful and stateless runs of the same system; its authors call it the first benchmark to do this across diverse real-world domains. MTOB is the best-known test of learning a skill from documents alone. What the proxy misses: CL-Bench has no human baseline yet, so 'professional pace' is not measured. Its sequences run 12 to 120 task instances, far short of the months a new hire spends, and its first round tested only memory kept in context, retrieval or notes, not weight updates such as test-time training. It cannot tell learning in the weights from notes kept in a memory file; we count both, since the definition only bars task-specific retraining. On MTOB, most of the gain comes from the book's example sentences rather than its grammar explanations. Tacit and social knowledge, such as how a particular team works, is not tested, and MTOB measures one skill learned in one sitting.

projection.text: No published trend exists for learning across tasks: CL-Bench is one snapshot from June 2026, and no newer models have been added since. Our METR time-horizon trend fit on Trend watch measures task length, not learning, so we do not extend it here. The clearest dated forecast we found is Dwarkesh Patel's 50/50 bet (June 2025) that AI learns on the job as well as a human, for any white-collar work, by 2032; his August 2026 essay on continual learning gives no new date and treats it as not yet working. Our read: the within-session part is moving fast (the best ARC-AGI-3 Standard-harness score rose from 0.51% in March to 62.7% in September 2026), while for the across-task part we have one data point and cannot yet tell its pace. A re-run of CL-Bench on the September 2026 models is the next data point that could start a trend.
projection.basis: Patel, 'Why I don't think AGI is right around the corner', June 2 2025, and '8 Predictions for the Era of Continual Learning', Aug 7 2026 (expert opinion); ARC Prize results from March and September 2026; CL-Bench, June 2026.
projection.ratingNote: Dwarkesh Patel's bet and essay are expert opinion; the sentences starting 'Our read' are our inference from ARC Prize's and CL-Bench's published results.

challenges.text: Learning in the weights is hard. Google Research says today's models know only what is in their context window or what they learned in pre-training, and that updating a model's parameters with new data often causes catastrophic forgetting of old skills. Its Nested Learning work (NeurIPS 2025) targets this problem.

Notes and memory do not yet add up to skill. On CL-Bench, agents often overfit to their latest observations or fail to reuse what they learned across instances, what an agent accumulates often hurts rather than helps, and plain in-context learning beats dedicated memory systems on most tasks.

Learning from its own feedback makes an agent drift. SkillLearnBench (Carnegie Mellon and Amazon AGI) finds every skill-learning method beats having no skills, but none leads across all tasks and models; repeated rounds help when feedback comes from outside, while self-feedback alone causes recursive drift.

Learning from documents may be narrower than it looks. A study of MTOB finds almost all of the translation gain comes from the grammar book's parallel example sentences, not its grammar explanations, and no evidence that long-context models use the explanations effectively (Aycock and colleagues, ICLR 2025).

There is a measurement gap. No benchmark we found has a human learning-pace baseline (Snorkel says it is working on one for some CL-Bench tasks), and the newest models (Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, Astra, Argon) are not on CL-Bench, so 'professional pace' cannot be checked yet.

components.hiddenAngle: Our inference. A hidden AGI (A) would need this component more than any other, and it is where public systems are weakest across tasks: 25.4% of the available gain on CL-Bench. Passing it in secret would therefore take a large unpublished jump. The component also ties to B and C. A system that keeps learning from its own work is one route to recursive self-improvement (B). A system running unseen in the economy (C) would need to adapt to new clients and tools; an operator could get partway there with external memory files, which leave no public trace. Four signs could show it. (1) A lab's next release jumps far beyond its predecessor on CL-Bench or on a human-baselined learning evaluation. (2) A deployed model's scores on fixed evaluations rise between announced versions, which would suggest undisclosed updates from deployment; re-runs by Artificial Analysis or CL-Bench could catch this. (3) A lab stops publishing continual-learning work it had been publishing, such as Google's Nested Learning line, while it keeps hiring for it. (4) Agents in the economy visibly improve on a client's own workflow over weeks without a model change. We have not seen any of these. Learning in the weights inside a lab, used only internally, would be hard to see from outside until a release or a disclosure (A, B). D does not depend on this component directly.

components.name: Generalization to the new
components.question: Can the system handle a kind of problem it has never seen before (new rules, a new game, a new field) about as well as a capable person working it out for the first time, not only the kinds of problems it was trained on?
components.clause: "generalize knowledge across any intellectual domain, without task-specific retraining" (v2.0); working component: "skilled-human performance on genuinely novel tasks and domains it wasn't trained for". Also inherits "no task-specific human scaffolding" from the v1.0 remote-work test (general harness only).

components.statusNote: Within three months of ARC-AGI-3's launch the best public score was 1.5%, against our 80%. Once the format was known, GPT-6 Astra reached 62.7% with the Standard harness (99.9% with the Provider Adapter) at about 27 to 37 times the paid human cost per game, and its lead did not carry over to WitnessBench's held-out games.
components.statusDetail: Partial by our rule: public models now solve new games once the format is known (GPT-6 Astra 62.7% on ARC-AGI-3's hidden set with the Standard harness and 99.9% with the Provider Adapter, at about 27 to 37 times the paid human cost per game, our calculation), but both parts of our test fail: the best score within three months of ARC-AGI-3's launch was 1.5%, and on WitnessBench's 17 held-out games the best of 18 models got through about 5 of 20 levels per game, with Astra's two-to-one ARC-AGI-3 lead over Claude Opus 5 not carrying over. Transfer to new professional fields is unmeasured.
components.bar: 80% on a new ARC generation within 3 months of its launch, at no more than 10 times human cost, with the lead holding on a held-out suite.

test.measure: Two parts, both under a general harness (no game- or task-specific code, prompts or tools). (1) Fresh-benchmark test: the score on ARC Prize's newest benchmark generation (ARC-AGI-3 today, ARC-AGI-4 next) on its hidden Semi-Private set with ARC's Standard harness, counting only models released before or within 3 months of the benchmark's public release. We show ARC's Provider Adapter results alongside: that harness adds the provider's own general context settings, not task-specific help, so whether it counts is the owner's call. (2) Transfer check: the same model's lead must hold, within error, on at least one independent held-out suite of the same kind that labs could not have trained on (today, WitnessBench's private test games), so a score cannot come from training on the genre alone.
test.threshold: Partial: a public system passes 50% on the newest ARC generation only after it has been public for months, or reaches 80% but fails the transfer check. Close: a model released before a new generation scores 50% or more at its launch. Met: 80% or more within 3 months of a new generation's launch, with the Standard harness, at no more than 10 times ARC's paid human cost, and the lead holds on an independent held-out suite.
test.detail: Met when, within 3 months of a new ARC generation's release, a public system scores at least 80% (our reliability bar) with the Standard harness, at no more than 10 times ARC's paid human cost per task (about $12.78 per attempted ARC-AGI-3 game, so about $128), and its lead holds on an independent held-out suite. Close: a model released before the new generation scores 50% or more at launch. Partial: systems pass 50% on the newest generation only after it has been public for months, or fail the transfer check. Far: below 50% even then. ARC scores 100% as beating every level of every game in no more actions than the median person who completed that level; on ARC-AGI-3's 25 public games 42% of first-time human plays were full solves, so we read 80% as a skilled first-time player, above a typical one (our inference; we found no published per-person score spread). ARC-AGI-3's 3-month window closed on June 25, 2026, so the earliest this can be met is ARC-AGI-4.
test.why: Each ARC generation went from near 0% to near saturation once labs could aim at it: ARC-AGI-1 in about 5 years (87.5% at 172 times the standard compute, Dec 2024), ARC-AGI-2 in about 13 months to 85%, ARC-AGI-3 in about 5 months to 99.9% with the Provider Adapter harness. So only a score on tasks that are new to the system says much about generalization rather than preparation. ARC Prize's own view is that AGI arrives when tasks easy for people and hard for AI can no longer be built; this test applies that one generation at a time. What it misses: ARC games are short, closed, deterministic puzzles that use only core-knowledge priors, and ARC Prize says ARC-AGI-3 'does not represent the complexity and open-endedness of the real world'. No public, contamination-controlled test of transfer to genuinely new professional fields exists, so we treat that part as unmeasured and say so.

milestones.text: François Chollet publishes 'On the Measure of Intelligence', defining intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency and introducing the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC, later ARC-AGI-1).

OpenAI's unreleased o3-preview, trained on 75% of ARC-AGI-1's public training set, scores 75.7% on the Semi-Private set within ARC's $10k limit (87.5% at 172 times the compute). ARC-AGI-1 had taken four years to go from 0% to 5%.
ARC-AGI-2 launches: pure LLMs score 0% and public reasoning systems single digits. Every task was solved by at least two people in two attempts or fewer; the average tester scored 60%.

ARC Prize 2025 results: no grand prize. On ARC-AGI-2's private set the best Kaggle entry scores 24% ($0.20 per task), the best verified commercial model (Claude Opus 4.5) 37.6%, the best refinement system (Poetiq on Gemini 3 Pro) 54%.

ARC-AGI-3 launches: 135 hand-made interactive games (25 public, 110 held back) with no instructions or stated goals. Every game was fully solved by at least two of the ten first-time testers who tried it; frontier AI scores 0.51%.

OpenAI releases GPT-5.5, and ARC Prize verifies 85.0% on ARC-AGI-2, the bar ARC set for its prize, about 13 months after launch (as a commercial system, not under the efficiency limits of the open-source prize).
Claude Opus 5 sets a new ARC-AGI-3 high of 30.2%; the previous high was 7.8% (GPT-5.6 Sol). ARC Prize attributes the gain to stronger logical reasoning.

A Fleet AI researcher reports that on Witness, his team's held-out set of ARC-AGI-3-style games, Opus 5's jump does not carry over: a statistical tie with Fable 5 and Kimi K3, and below Opus 4.8 on the most novel game.

GPT-6 Astra scores 62.7% on ARC-AGI-3 with ARC's Standard harness and 99.9% with the Provider Adapter harness. ARC Prize calls it 'meaningful progress towards generalization' but says it is not claiming AGI and that ARC-AGI-3 does not represent real-world open-endedness.

Chollet calls Astra 'a major breakthrough in model intelligence', says harness capabilities are 'increasingly shifting into the model itself' and progress came about twice as fast as he expected, and adds that solving ARC-AGI-3 'is not proof of AGI'.

WitnessBench is published: on its 17 held-out games the best of 18 models, Claude Fable 5, clears about 5 of 20 levels; on the first five levels GPT-6 Astra (27.6) trails Opus 5 (30.6) and Fable 5 (36.4).

projection.text: No published trend or forecast covers first-contact generalization, so we give no date of our own. Expert views: François Chollet, who designs the ARC series, plans benchmarks 'until it is no longer possible to propose something that humans can do and AI can't' and wrote 'AGI ~2030' (Feb 12, 2026); after Astra he said the progress came 'about 2x faster than I anticipated' (Sept 3). ARC Prize says ARC-AGI-4 will test autonomous open-ended innovation (Sept 12), and Chollet said in March it would be released in early 2027, which makes it the first real test of our threshold. Our reading of ARC's data: the time from a generation's launch to a public score above 80% fell from about 5 years (ARC-AGI-1) to about 11 months (ARC-AGI-2) to about 5 months (ARC-AGI-3, Provider Adapter harness only), but the best score in the first three months stayed low (about 9% on ARC-AGI-2, 1.5% on ARC-AGI-3). We would call the component close only if that early gap shrinks.

challenges.text: Benchmarks stop measuring novelty once they become targets. ARC Prize's own ARC-AGI-3 paper warns that tests built to resist memorization 'can now be attacked via higher-level shortcuts' by training on masses of look-alike tasks, and its testing policy says the Semi-Private games, which are sent to lab APIs, may leak over time. GPT-6 Astra's knowledge cutoff (Apr 30, 2026, per OpenAI) is five weeks after ARC-AGI-3's public launch. How much of each generation's rise came from training on the genre is unknown (our reading).

With a code-running harness, the PRO-LONG paper reports Fable 5 at 97.4% (best of 2) on the 25 public games for $1,750, and an average 18-point gain over a base coding agent across frontier models. It is hard to separate the model's generalization from the harness's (our reading).

In the one fully controlled study we found, small transformers (2 to 8 layers) trained from scratch on an arithmetic-program grammar lost over 30% when they had to write syntactically novel programs, and gains from more compute were log-linear. It did not test frontier models; we cite it as a reason for caution, not a measurement of them (our reading).

components.hiddenAngle: A hidden system that generalized at skilled-human level would be hard to see in public benchmarks. ARC Prize tests models at its own discretion, mostly public ones, and publishes an unreleased model's result no later than 30 days after public release, so a model that is never released need never appear (testing policy). There is precedent: ARC Prize scored OpenAI's unreleased o3-preview in December 2024. OpenAI says an unreleased internal model is 'significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra' (Sept 8), and no ARC or other outside evaluation of it is listed. In March Chollet called ARC-AGI-3 an 'early warning signal': 'any sudden score jump will mean something important has changed about AI capabilities'. Observable traces: (A) a lab or ARC Prize disclosing a first-contact score on ARC-AGI-4 or a held-out suite well above the best public model, or a public model arriving with a near-human launch-day score, which would imply an internal predecessor had it earlier; (B) launch-to-saturation time shrinking from about 5 months toward weeks alongside lab claims of automated research, since fast adaptation to new tasks is what recursive self-improvement needs; (C) agents adapting covertly inside unfamiliar real systems beyond the sub-AGI incidents we track (so far all trace to sub-AGI agents or human operators); (D) only indirectly linked. Because labs can train toward any published genre, a strong public ARC score alone is not evidence of hidden AGI and a low one is not evidence against it; first-contact and held-out results are the signals we trust most.

statusRule: Each part's test publishes its Partial, Close and Met marks (test.threshold). A part's status is the highest mark the best public evidence reaches. A part passed on the overall figure only does not count as passed. Unreleased-model results never set a status.

A.name: Hidden AGI
A.text: A system meets our definition of AGI (definitions v2.0), and whoever built it, a company or a government program, has kept that level of capability from the public for at least 30 days. Admitting that an unreleased model exists doesn't count as disclosure.

B.name: Hidden self-improvement
B.text: An AI system does most of the work of building a more capable successor, with at least a 3x speed-up over humans alone, and whoever runs it, a company or a government program, has kept this from the public for at least 30 days. Partial AI-driven acceleration is already public, so it doesn't count. B does not need AGI.

C.name: Covert AGI actor
C.text: An AGI-level system takes sustained actions online or in the economy, and the public hasn't known for at least 30 days, on either of two paths: sanctioned but undisclosed (its developer or another operator runs it on purpose and doesn't say so), or rogue or stolen (it acts outside its developer's control). Agent incidents below AGI level are warning signs, not proof.

D.name: Covert government influence
D.text: Output from an AGI-level system materially shapes a major government decision without the public knowing. Heavy government use of tools below AGI level doesn't count.

Dopen.name: Open government influence
Dopen.text: The same through acknowledged government use, even of a system whose AGI-level capability hasn't been disclosed. It is outside the Index, which counts only hidden scenarios.
